transcript:
Header: 2026-12-08 15:30 UTC | Duration: 56 mins | Attendees: Aisha, Marcus, Priya (Redwood) / Liam, Sandra, Raj (NovusAI)

[00:00] Aisha: thanks everyone for joining, we know it's a busy week so we'll run through migration parity, show the Console and Optimize tips, and set next steps. is this still focused on migrating from OpenAI and Together models?
[00:10] Liam: yes, we have a mix, mostly OpenAI GPT-4 style endpoints and a few Together models for lower latency scoring, and anthro--anthropic for safety checks on some customer facing flows.
[00:25] Marcus: cool, so i'll do the parity mapping first, quick note on names: we map GPT-family to our rwd-gpt-4-v1 type profiles, Together small models map to rwd-llm-small quantized profiles, and anthropic claude-like workloads map to our high-context safety variants, there are some nuance on tokenization and stop sequences.
[00:40] Sandra: can you show an example api call? our infra uses streaming and function calling heavily.
[00:50] Marcus: yep. OpenAI call uses model, temperature, max_tokens, stop. In Redwood the call shape is very similar but a few keys differ, and we support streaming with the same events. Example: POST /v1/generate with engine rwd-gpt-4-v1, body includes messages, temperature, top_p, and optional tools array for function calling. There is also a route-level config in the Console for defaults, so you dont need to set everything in code.
[01:15] Raj: any gotchas on retries and kv cache when you do streaming? we have long conversations and use kv cache heavily.
[01:25] Marcus: good point. our runtime keeps a kv cache that persists across tokens in a request and we expose session caching options. The main migration note is how you pass the prior KV context - in OpenAI you pass full messages; in Redwood you can attach a session_id to leverage prefix caching which reduces token cost. So you'll likely see cost drop on repeated prompts.
[01:45] Liam: what about quality parity, like are completions identical if we use same temperature and prompts?
[01:50] Marcus: identical is tricky - we aim for parity but model weights differ. Our parity mapping doc lists recommended parameter adjustments, e.g. temperature off by 0.05, nucleus sampling tweaks, and deterministic seeding options. For Anthropic style assistant patterns we recommend using the safety prompt templates in the Console.
[02:10] Sandra: security concerns: we need SOC2, SSO, KMS and control plane in our VPC. Can Redwood do that?
[02:20] Priya: yes, on Private we support VPC peering and an optional on-prem package. We integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key material, SAML SSO for auth, and have audit logs streaming to your SIEM. We also have SOC2 Type II and ISO in our compliance docs - we'll share the pack.
[02:40] Liam: good. pricing question: how do tokens and dedicated capacity interplay? we need predictable throughput for peak times.
[02:50] Aisha: hosted is usage-based, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput with monthly commits. For peak bursting you can configure burst capacity. We'll send a pricing example based on your 1M token estimate.
[03:05] Raj: demo the Console?
[03:10] Aisha: yep i'll share my screen.
[03:15] [screen share noise, small delay]
[03:25] Aisha: Console home -- per-route charts, latency p95, token cost breakdown, and a routing policy screen. Here you can pin a route to a model family, and set fallback to cheaper model variants on overload, which helps with graceful degradation.
[03:45] Sandra: can we set teams and RBAC?
[03:50] Aisha: yes, RBAC at org and project level, SSO integration. You can also restrict which models a team can call.
[04:05] Marcus: switching back to API parity -- Together uses a slightly different tokenization and some stop token behaviours. For 'together' you may be passing chat roles in a different shape; our mapping guide shows a small shim: map roles to message role strings and use stream=true. Example mapping file: together_message -> {role: system|user|assistant, content: text} -> Redwood messages array. We will attach a sample script in the parity doc.
[04:35] Liam: we rely on function calling heavily to call downstream microservices and to do structured outputs, is that supported?
[04:45] Marcus: yes, function/tool calling supported. We return structured json and you can register tools in the Console. There's also a function-calling debug view for payloads. One caveat: schema strictness is optional but recommended for safety.
[05:05] Sandra: what about embeddings? we use embeddings for retrieval and reranking across hundreds of millions of docs.
[05:15] Priya: embeddings endpoints have parity for vector dims and we provide batch endpoints plus incremental upsert via the console. We also provide recommendations in Optimize for quantized embeddings and caching strategies.
[05:35] Liam: ok benchmarks, how should we run them?
[05:40] Marcus: two options: we can run a Redwood-hosted benchmark on a small sample you provide, or give you a script to run in your env that hits our dedicated or hosted endpoints. For fairness we recommend identical prompts, warm cache, and measure p50/p95 latency and tokens/unit cost. We will run the first pass and share results.
[06:05] Raj: any migration pitfalls? specifically with stop sequences and streaming deltas.
[06:12] Marcus: streaming event framing differs slightly; stop token behaviours may need a small change, e.g. explicit stop array vs hint stop. We list common pitfall items in parity doc. Also watch for rate limits - your client libraries may need rate limiter tweaks because Redwood supports higher sustained QPS on Dedicated.
[06:35] Sandra: one more on data residency, we need EU-only processing for a subset.
[06:40] Priya: you can pin routes to region and on Private we can deploy in your VPC in eu-west-1. We'll include the deployment checklist.
[06:55] Liam: about model variants and quantization, will we see quality drop if you recommend int8 quantized variants?
[07:05] Marcus: there's a tradeoff. Optimize suggests which layers and profiles are safe to quantize given your workload. For chatty prompts we often keep key layers in fp16 and quantize others. We'll share a recommended quantization profile for your prompt patterns.
[07:30] Sandra: how do we do A/B between current OpenAI models and Redwood? can we route traffic?
[07:35] Aisha: yes, routing policies allow canary and A/B with automatic fallback. You can set percentage rollouts and compare metrics in Console.
[07:50] [minor cross talk]
[08:00] Marcus: one practical demo snippet -- here's a sample curl that shows parity: curl POST /v1/generate, header Authorization, body messages array. We show both streaming and non-streaming payloads. If you use our SDK it's even easier, few lines to swap model name and session id.
[08:20] Raj: is there an SDK for Node/python?
[08:25] Aisha: yes, we have both and examples for mapping OpenAI calls to Redwood. we'll include those in the repo link.
[08:35] Liam: any long tail issues with safety outputs when switching from Anthropic? some of our safety pipelines rely on claude style responses.
[08:45] Priya: we provide safety templates and a safety layer in Optimize that can run post-generation checks and rerank. For strict compliance you can chain both: Redwood generation -> safety reranker -> final. This is identical pattern to what you do today but with our hooks for latency.
[09:10] Sandra: how are logs and PII handled?
[09:15] Priya: you can disable retention, or have logs routed to your SIEM. Private gives you full control. We also support token redaction and encrypted audit logs via KMS.
[09:35] Marcus: quick note on costs -- Optimize will recommend batching windows, prefix caching and quantization that together can reduce cost per token significantly. Example: for chat history heavy workloads, prefix caching reduces repeated tokens by up to 40% in our internal tests.
[09:55] Liam: great. anything else in Console?
[10:00] Aisha: model catalog shows performance profiles and recommended route configs. Also an eval harness section where you can upload prompt sets and compare outputs side-by-side. That should help with parity validation.
[10:20] Raj: ok demo looks good. what do you need from us to run the benchmark?
[10:25] Marcus: sample prompt set, representative history lengths, expected QPS, and token volume estimate. We'll run warm runs and cold to show differences.
[10:40] Liam: we can provide 500 sample prompts first.
[10:42] Aisha: perfect. we'll follow up with a ticket to collect those.
[10:50] Sandra: timeline question -- if pilot goes well how long to production?
[10:55] Aisha: depends on Dedicated and Private decisions -- hosted quick to move in weeks, Dedicated 4-8 weeks for capacity and contracts, Private varies by network but 6-12 weeks typically. We'll map a timeline after pilot.
[11:15] Marcus: any final technical deep dives requested?
[11:20] Raj: yes, may want an SE deep dive on kv cache semantics and session_id usage.
[11:25] Aisha: noted, Marcus will follow up for an SE deep dive.
[11:30] [wrap up] Aisha: recap: we'll send parity mapping doc, sample SDK mappings, pricing and Dedicated options; Marcus will run benchmark and share results; Novus will share 500 sample prompts. schedule pilot kickoff 12/15. thanks everyone.

End transcript.

References and shared artifacts: parity-mapping.pdf (link to share), sdk-mapping-examples.zip, benchmark-template.csv.
